title: Can We Trust the Manuscripts?
subtitle: Textual criticism for beginners. The variants honestly counted, and what they do and do not touch.
triageNote: Whether God has preserved his word is a weighty matter, and every Christian position on this page says yes. The in-house question, which family of manuscripts best preserves it and which printed Greek text should sit under our translations, is the kind of difference that lives peaceably inside one congregation. There the man with the King James and the woman with the ESV share a pew and a Lord. The skeptical challenge is another matter, and is answered here at full strength. A church that cannot answer it honestly will answer it dishonestly, and the dishonest answers are the ones that cost people their faith later.
question: No original manuscript of any biblical book survives. What survives is copies, of copies, of copies. Roughly 5,800 catalogued Greek manuscripts of the New Testament in whole or part. Some ten thousand more in Latin, thousands more in Coptic, Syriac, and other languages, plus the biblical quotations that saturate the church fathers. No two manuscripts agree exactly. The differences between them are called variants, and the best current estimates put the total around half a million. Textual criticism is the discipline that compares the copies to establish, as nearly as possible, the original wording. The question of this page is the one your neighbor asks on the porch. With no originals and half a million variants, can you honestly claim to know what the New Testament said. And inside the church, a second question: by what method, and from which manuscripts, should we decide.
whyItMatters:
In 2005 Bart Ehrman, a fine textual scholar who began as an evangelical, published Misquoting Jesus, and it became the rare bestseller about Greek manuscripts. Millions of readers met, for the first time, facts that are perfectly true. The originals are gone, the copies disagree, scribes made errors and sometimes changes. And a handful of beloved passages, the woman caught in adultery, the long ending of Mark, were almost certainly not written by the evangelists. Many of those readers had been taught a doctrine of Scripture with no room for any of this. The collision was shipwreck. That collision is preventable, and prevention is called textual criticism, taught before the crisis instead of after.

It matters in the other direction too. Some Christian apologetics oversells, waving manuscript counts like a weapon. It never mentions that most of those manuscripts are medieval, or that the count of variants is large precisely because the count of copies is. The skeptic eventually checks, and oversell discovered becomes distrust compounded. The actual situation, stated without varnish, is strong enough that it needs no varnish. The New Testament is, by any measure, the best-attested text of the ancient world. Its variants are overwhelmingly trivial. The meaningful exceptions are known, listed, and printed in the footnotes of your own Bible, and no doctrine of the Christian faith rests on a disputed reading. Learning why those sentences are true, and where their honest edges are, is this page's whole business.

And it matters at the pew level because of the footnotes themselves. Sooner or later a reader finds the bracket at Mark 16, or the note at John 8, and wonders what else the editors know. The answer is: nothing hidden. Textual criticism is the rare field where the entire evidence is published, the disagreements are catalogued in the open, and the reader can check. That openness is not the faith's embarrassment. It is one of its credentials.

positions.name: Reasoned eclecticism, the mainstream method
positions.inOneLine: Weigh each variant case by case, preferring the reading best supported by the oldest and most widespread witnesses and best able to explain how the others arose. The resulting text is the New Testament to a margin of doubt too small to matter doctrinally.
positions.bestCase:
Let me show you the embarrassment of riches first, because the scale is the argument. For Homer's Iliad, the best-attested work of classical antiquity after the New Testament, something under two thousand manuscripts survive. For Tacitus, our principal historian of first-century Rome, portions of his Annals hang on a pair of medieval manuscripts. For the New Testament: roughly 5,800 Greek manuscripts, the versions in Latin and Syriac and Coptic by the thousands. The patristic quotations are so dense that the bulk of the New Testament could be reassembled from the fathers alone. And the trail starts early. P52, a credit-card-sized scrap of John in the John Rylands Library, is commonly dated to the first half of the second century, within a few decades of composition. Substantial papyri of the Gospels and Paul come from around 200. Complete New Testaments, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, stand in the fourth century. Between an ancient author and our first good copies there is usually a gulf of many centuries. For the New Testament it is a generation or two at the near edge. No other ancient text is in the same building.

Now the variants, counted honestly, because the half-million number is true and routinely misunderstood. The count is enormous because the evidence is enormous. Count the same itacism, the same slipped letter, across thousands of copies and the tally climbs by itself. Peter Gurry's careful 2016 estimate put non-spelling variants around half a million, and the great majority of even those are word-order shuffles and synonyms that cannot be rendered differently in English. Daniel Wallace's summary holds across the discipline: the variants that are both meaningful and viable, that change sense and have a real claim to originality, are far less than one percent of the whole. They are catalogued, every one, in apparatuses any reader can buy. Our method with each is simple to state and demanding to practice: prefer the reading that the oldest and most geographically scattered witnesses support, and that best explains the rise of its rivals. Scribes smoothed grammar, harmonized parallels, and expanded titles of reverence far more often than they roughened them. The reading that explains the others is the spring. The others are the streams.

What does the method yield. A Greek text, the Nestle-Aland, now in its twenty-eighth edition, whose differences from its rivals would fit on a few pages and affect no article of any creed. Yes, we print the famous brackets. Mark 16:9-20 and John 7:53-8:11 are absent from the earliest and best witnesses, and honesty puts them in the margin where the evidence puts them. Notice that nothing in either passage, and nothing in any seriously disputed variant, carries a doctrine not taught elsewhere on undisputed ground. Bruce Metzger knew this evidence as well as any man of his century. He said his decades among the variants deepened rather than weakened his confidence that the text in our hands is, in all essentials, the text the apostles wrote. That is not piety overriding scholarship. That is the scholarship.
advocates: the editors of the Nestle-Aland and UBS Greek texts

positions.name: Byzantine priority
positions.inOneLine: The text preserved in the great majority of manuscripts, the Byzantine tradition the church copied for a thousand years, is the most reliable witness to the original. The modern preference for a few early Egyptian copies is a methodological mistake.
positions.bestCase:
I want you to question one assumption, the one the whole modern edifice rests on: that older manuscript means better text. It sounds obvious. It is not. An early manuscript is early evidence for what one scribe in one place wrote. It is not automatically good evidence for what the apostles wrote. The handful of early papyri we possess come overwhelmingly from one province, Egypt, whose dry sand preserves what other climates destroy. They testify to the text of Egypt, copied with Egyptian habits, some of them frankly carelessly. And the two great fourth-century codices the critical text leans on, Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, disagree with each other thousands of times in the Gospels alone. Building the New Testament chiefly on that narrow regional base is like reconstructing American English from the surviving letters of one county.

Now consider what I build on instead. The New Testament was copied continuously, publicly, and under use, in the Greek-speaking church. That church never lost the language, never lost the liturgy, and read these books aloud every week from the apostles' day to the fall of Constantinople in 1453. That continuous stream left us thousands of manuscripts in remarkable agreement, the Byzantine text. Maurice Robinson's argument, and mine, is transmissional. In a normal copying process, the original reading is present from the start in every line of transmission. It tends to dominate the tradition numerically, while any particular error or local revision, however early, remains a tributary. To overthrow the united testimony of the stream, you need more than two old codices from one region and a method that prizes the harder reading. That canon, applied with enough confidence, will eventually prefer scribal blunders on principle, because blunders are always the harder reading.

Let me also relieve you of a misconception: this is not the King James position in academic dress. The Byzantine-priority case is argued on the same evidence, in the same journals, by the same methods of weighing witnesses. Where the late printed Textus Receptus departs from the majority of manuscripts, as it does in famous places, I depart from the Textus Receptus. Nor is the practical difference between my text and the critical text large. We agree far more than we differ, and I cheerfully echo my colleagues, no doctrine rides on the differences. What rides on it is a principle of method and, frankly, a theology of preservation. Is God's keeping of his word better sought in the church's whole, continuous, public tradition of copying, or in whatever happened to survive in one dry corner of the empire. I think the stream, not the sandbank, and I am content to let the argument be judged by the evidence, where it has been gaining ground for forty years.
advocates: Zane Hodges and Arthur Farstad (The Greek New Testament According to the Majority Text, 1982)
the long tradition of the Greek-speaking church

positions.name: The confessional Textus Receptus position
positions.inOneLine: God promised to preserve his word and did so in the text the church actually used and confessed, the Hebrew Masoretic text and the Greek Textus Receptus underlying the Reformation Bibles. So the search for a better text misreads both the promise and the church's history.
positions.bestCase:
My position begins where the others do not, with doctrine. The words of the Lord are pure words, says Psalm 12, kept and preserved forever. Heaven and earth will pass away, says the Lord, but my words will not pass away. The Westminster Confession of 1646 drew the consequence in one clause that is the charter of my view: the Old Testament in Hebrew and the New Testament in Greek, being immediately inspired by God, were by his singular care and providence kept pure in all ages. Kept pure in all ages. Not lost for fifteen centuries and recovered by Victorian professors. Not waiting in a monastery wastebasket for Tischendorf's visit in 1844, nor in a Vatican cupboard, but kept, in the church's open, public, used Bible. Preservation through the church's use is how a covenant God keeps covenant documents.

Think through what the alternative concedes. The two pillars of the modern critical text, Vaticanus and Sinaiticus, were essentially outside the church's use for a millennium and a half. Take the readings they carry, where they differ from the received text. The body of Christ did not read them, did not preach them, and did not confess them through the entire age of the creeds, the Reformation, and the great missionary expansions. When Westcott and Hort enthroned those two witnesses in 1881, the church made a trade. She swapped a text validated by universal, continuous ecclesiastical use for a text validated by the accidents of survival and the judgments of academics. She accepted with it a principle she has been living with ever since: that the true wording of God's word is provisional, pending the next papyrus, the next edition, the next committee vote. I decline the principle. A perpetually revisable Bible is a Bible held on lease from the academy, and faith cannot stand at parade rest waiting for the twenty-ninth edition.

So I receive the Textus Receptus, the Greek text printed from Erasmus in 1516 through the Elzevirs in 1633, the text under the Geneva Bible and the King James Version. Not because Erasmus was inspired, he was not. Not because I cannot read an apparatus, I can. I receive it because that text is, in substance, the Byzantine text of the church's long use. It was providentially gathered and set in type at the very moment God was reforming his church and sending her Bible into all the world's languages. Men point to its famous seams, the Johannine Comma of 1 John 5:7, the readings with thin Greek support. I answer that my confidence rests not on the textual pedigree of each reading taken alone but on the providence of God over the whole. That is the same providence the mainstream view quietly invokes when it assures you nothing essential was lost. Every position on this page trusts providence somewhere. I trust it where the Confession placed it, in the text the church confessed, and I am unembarrassed to say so out loud.
advocates: Edward F. Hills (The King James Version Defended, 1956)
confessional Reformed and Baptist circles holding the Westminster and 1689 standards strictly

positions.name: The skeptical challenge
positions.inOneLine: With the originals gone, the earliest copies generations removed, and the text demonstrably altered by scribes with theological motives, what we possess is the church's text. Confidence about the apostles' exact words is misplaced.
positions.bestCase:
I will state my case with the discipline's own facts, since I helped catalogue them. We do not have the originals. We do not have copies of the originals, nor copies of those. For most New Testament books, our earliest substantial witnesses stand a century or more from composition. And the second century, the very period when copying was least controlled, done by amateurs, under no central oversight, is precisely the period from which almost nothing survives. By the time the manuscript record becomes rich, in the fourth century, the text had already passed through its most vulnerable years in the dark. The confident reconstructions you have heard tonight reconstruct the text as it emerged from that tunnel. What entered the tunnel is, strictly, beyond demonstration.

And we know the scribes changed things, not merely slipped, because we can watch them do it. The angry Jesus of Mark 1:41 becomes compassionate in the later tradition. Luke's account of the agony in Gethsemane gains the sweat like drops of blood, in a passage missing from key early witnesses and suspiciously useful against those who denied the Lord's true humanity. The Johannine Comma, the one explicit Trinitarian proof-text in the tradition, enters the Greek Bible in the sixteenth century with essentially no ancient Greek support. It stood in the most printed verse lists of Protestant orthodoxy for four hundred years. My book on this was called The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture for a reason. The alterations are not random noise. They cluster where doctrine was contested. The text was, at the margins, a participant in the church's controversies, not a sealed exhibit above them. Add the two facts every honest apparatus admits, that variants outnumber the words of the New Testament severalfold, and that in some places the editors themselves print diamonds of uncertainty. My conclusion is modest, not wild: we possess a very old, very interesting, humanly transmitted text, and the doctrine of a verbally inspired original is a doctrine about a document nobody has.

Now, because this page deals fairly, I will tell you what I tell my own audiences when they get overexcited. The textual critics and I agree on perhaps ninety-nine percent of the wording. I co-wrote the standard textbook with Metzger and stand by it. In the appendix to my own bestseller I answered a direct question directly: essential Christian beliefs are not affected by textual variants in the manuscript tradition of the New Testament. My challenge was never that the church secretly lost the gospel in the copying. It is sharper and smaller. The doctrine many of you were raised on, an inerrant text kept word-perfect by God, is falsified by the visible history of the words. A faith built on that doctrine is built on a vacancy. If your faith can say, with open eyes, that God worked through an ordinary, errant, human copying process, you and I have little left to fight about. And you did not learn that posture from the apologetics that promised you certainty.
advocates: Bart D. Ehrman (Misquoting Jesus, 2005; The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, 1993)
David C. Parker (The Living Text of the Gospels, 1997)
a broad stream of secular and post-confessional scholarship
keyTexts: Jeremiah 8:8 (the false pen of the scribes)

biblicalEvidence.summary: The words of the Lord are pure words. You shall keep them, O Lord, you shall preserve them from this generation forever. Read as a direct promise of the verbal preservation of Scripture through all ages.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for views with no doctrine of preservation at all, and contested ground for everyone, because the Hebrew is genuinely ambiguous.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Hebrew pronouns in verse 7 most naturally refer back to the poor and needy of verse 5, God preserving his persecuted people, not his words. The mainstream and Byzantine positions read it so, noting that the same psalmists who praise God's words never name a mechanism of manuscript transmission. The confessional position answers that the nearer antecedent is the words of verse 6, and that the Jewish and Christian reading tradition has long heard both. Even taken of the saints, the psalm's logic, God keeps what is his, applies with equal force to his words. The skeptic observes that the debate over what this verse itself says is conducted across manuscript traditions, which rather makes his point.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. The Lord's own statements of the permanence of God's words, down to the smallest stroke.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the skeptical position if permanence implies preservation, and pressed by confessional writers against any view that locates the true text in lost autographs rather than the church's living possession.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Reasoned eclecticism reads both texts as promises of enduring authority and fulfillment, the Law accomplished, the words vindicated, not as predictions about copyist accuracy. The iota saying concerns the Law's validity until fulfillment, not the spelling of future manuscripts. The skeptic notes, fairly, that whatever the verses promise, the empirical history of the copies includes real loss and real change. Any doctrine of preservation must be compatible with the manuscripts we actually have. The confessional reply: it is, that is the point, the words never passed away, because the church never lost them.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Reasoned eclecticism, as the discipline's showcase
biblicalEvidence.summary: The long ending of Mark, with the snake-handling and poison-drinking promises, is absent from Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, unknown to several early fathers' texts, and stylistically distinct. Most scholars judge it a second-century addition, and modern Bibles bracket it with a note.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the confessional position, which receives the passage. Hard too for naive doctrines of transmission in every camp, since either an ending was added by the church or one was lost from the earliest copies.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Byzantine position defends the passage's originality with real arguments. It stands in the vast majority of manuscripts. It was cited by Irenaeus around 180, a century before our earliest omitting witnesses, and the abrupt alternative, a Gospel ending mid-sentence at fear, is itself a difficulty. The confessional position receives it on the church's continuous use. Reasoned eclecticism answers Irenaeus with the combined silence of the best early evidence and the seam in style. It draws the pastoral moral all sides can keep: the resurrection it narrates is taught beyond dispute in the other Gospels and in Paul. That is why this, the largest variant in the New Testament, holds no doctrine hostage.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: Reasoned eclecticism, with everyone instructed by it
biblicalEvidence.summary: The woman caught in adultery is missing from every early Greek manuscript, floats to different locations in later ones, sometimes appearing after Luke 21:38, and interrupts John's narrative seam. Nearly all textual scholars, including conservative ones, judge it a later insertion, while many also suspect it preserves a true story about Jesus.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for the confessional position, and emotionally hard for everyone, because it is among the most beloved passages in the Bible.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: The Byzantine position is divided here, candidly, since even the majority tradition transmits the passage unevenly. Robinson has studied its hundreds of manuscripts more closely than anyone while defending its place in the tradition. The skeptic uses it as Exhibit A that the church's Bible grew. The eclectic answer doubles as the confessional comfort. The passage was marked with obeli, doubt-signs, by honest Byzantine scribes themselves, and the church has always handled it with a footnote's care. No teaching of Christ's mercy rests on it alone, Luke 7 and Luke 15 carry the same Lord.

biblicalEvidence.leansToward: The skeptical challenge and reasoned eclecticism together
biblicalEvidence.summary: The explicitly Trinitarian wording, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost, and these three are one, appears in no Greek manuscript before the late Middle Ages. It entered printed Bibles when Erasmus included it in his third edition of 1522 after criticism for omitting it, and stood in the King James Version. It is the clearest case of a late reading achieving canonical circulation.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Very hard for the confessional Textus Receptus position, which must defend the Comma or qualify its principle, and a standing caution against proof-texting for everyone.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Confessional writers like Hills defend it through the Latin tradition's antiquity and providential-use reasoning, conceding the Greek evidence and relocating the argument to providence. Critics inside and outside the camp judge that the position's least persuasive moment. The mainstream and Byzantine views agree the Comma is not original. They note what its removal costs doctrine: nothing, the Trinity being established from Matthew 28:19, John 1, 2 Corinthians 13:14, and the whole grain of the New Testament. That is itself the standing lesson, that no doctrine was ever one variant deep.

biblicalEvidence.summary: Luke describes sources, eyewitness tradition, careful investigation, and orderly writing, so that Theophilus may have certainty about the things he was taught. The New Testament's own picture of how its text relates to history: through human diligence God is pleased to use.
biblicalEvidence.hardFor: Hard for any doctrine of the text, conservative or skeptical, that has no room for ordinary human process inside God's provision.
biblicalEvidence.howOthersRead: Every Christian position claims this verse comfortably, which is instructive. The same providence that worked through Luke's research can work through scribes and through the critics who compare their copies, and the eclectic critic sees his own discipline as Luke's diligence continued. The skeptic reads it as the first link in a wholly human chain. The difference between those two readings is not in the evidence. It is in the doctrine of providence each brings to it, which is worth admitting on all sides.

weighing:
My judgment, tentatively held, and I will show my work.

On the method question, I find reasoned eclecticism the most honest broker. It is the only position whose evidence and reasoning are entirely on the table, every variant published, every judgment argued in the open. And its results have absorbed a century and a half of new papyri without a single discovery dislodging anything that matters. The Byzantine men have landed real blows. The Egyptian narrowness of the early evidence is a fair point, and I am glad their argument sits inside the discipline keeping it honest. The confessional position I honor for taking preservation seriously as doctrine, and I part from it where the Comma forces the choice between the principle and the evidence. A providence that must defend a sixteenth-century reading against the whole ancient Greek tradition has become a providence of the printing press. I cannot find that in the Confession's intent, let alone in Scripture.

On the skeptic, let me say what I actually think, since this page exists for the reader he has shaken. Nearly every fact in his case is true, and nearly every weight he hangs on the facts is wrong. It is true the originals are gone, as they are for every ancient text. It is true the dark second century limits demonstrative certainty. It is true that scribes sometimes bent words toward doctrine, and the discipline he helped build caught them doing it. That is the part of the story he undersells: we know about Mark 1:41 and Luke 22:43 and the Comma because the method works. His own bottom line, conceded in his own appendix, that no essential Christian belief is affected, is the bottom line. A reader who walks away from the faith over the difference between a ninety-nine percent text and a hundred percent text was given, somewhere, a faith calibrated wrong. He was taught to need a kind of certainty God evidently did not choose to give. He gave us this manuscript tradition and not another.

And that is my settled, tentative conclusion: the manuscript history we actually have looks like the rest of God's ordinary providence, abundant, human, uneven, self-correcting, and sufficient. Not a golden tablet. A tradition, kept by the same God who runs the rest of history through means. I trust the text in my hands for the same reason Metzger trusted it after sixty years closer to the evidence than I will ever stand. The footnotes are not cracks in the foundation. They are the receipts.
charitableDisagreement:
Inside the church, this is third-order, and it should feel like it. The eclectic critic is guarding honesty, the principle that the people of the truth must never need the evidence trimmed. The Byzantine scholar is guarding the church's continuous tradition against the tyranny of the latest find. The confessional brother is guarding the doctrine of preservation and the settled Bible of the pew against a text forever in beta. These three should be able to share a communion rail, and in healthy churches they do. The congregation that fights over Bible versions is almost never really fighting over manuscripts. It is fighting over trust, and the cure is teaching, the very teaching this page attempts.

Toward the skeptic, charity means granting his facts, thanking him for the discipline he practices with real skill, and disputing the sermon he preaches from the facts. It also means absorbing his fair rebuke: parts of the church did promise people a kind of textual certainty the manuscripts do not offer, and when the promise broke, it broke people. The remedy is not louder promises. It is the truth at full strength. A text attested beyond any ancient rival, variants counted in the open, the meaningful ones footnoted in the Bible on your shelf, and not one article of the creed in their keeping. Die on the hill that God has spoken and that his word has reached you. Do not die on the hill of a textual theory, and never, ever win an argument for the Bible with a claim the evidence cannot keep. The Lord of truth is not honored by exaggeration, even in his defense.

relatedDebates.note: Careful inerrancy statements attach to the original manuscripts. That makes the relationship between autograph and copy a load-bearing wall in that doctrine. Whether inerrancy-of-autographs plus reliability-of-copies adds up to a trustworthy Bible in hand is argued on the inerrancy page of this set.

Some differences between Bible versions are textual, the KJV following the Textus Receptus where modern versions follow the critical text. Most are translational. Telling the two apart dissolves a large share of pew-level confusion, and the translations page takes up the rest.

relatedDebates.topic: The reliability of the Gospels as history
relatedDebates.note: Textual criticism establishes what the documents said. The further question is whether what they said is true. That case, from undesigned coincidences to the evidence of names and geography, is made accessibly in Peter Williams's Can We Trust the Gospels and Blomberg's work on the historical reliability of the Gospels.
